entities.summary: Crates of Athens (b. 400 BCE) was a prominent philosopher and thinker of the Classical era, active in the Global region. He is known for his contributions to the fields of philosophy and the Epicurean school, which emphasized the pursuit of happiness and the avoidance of pain through the cultivation of friendships and the rejection of superstition. Crates of Athens was a key figure associated with the Epicurean school, which was founded by Epicurus in 341 BCE in Athens, Greece. The school's teachings had a significant impact on Western philosophy, influencing many prominent thinkers, including the Stoic school's founder, Zeno of Citium. The Epicurean school's emphasis on friendship and the rejection of superstition resonated with Crates of Athens' own views on the importance of human relationships and the limitations of human knowledge. Crates of Athens' critiques of the Stoic school, which he saw as overly rigid and dogmatic, contributed to the development of the Hellenistic philosophical tradition. He was also known for his critiques of the social and political systems of ancient Greece, which he saw as corrupt and unjust. Crates of Athens' ideas had a lasting impact on Western philosophy, influencing many prominent thinkers, including the Roman statesman and philosopher, Cicero. His ideas on the importance of friendship and the rejection of superstition continue to be studied and debated by scholars today.
